title: Chinese company reportedly building its own DUV chipmaking machines, and that's a really big deal
summary: Meanwhile, the US still hopes to block ASML from selling and servicing similar machines in China.
body: A Chinese state-backed company has begun mass producing deep ultraviolet lithography machines, reports The Information . That's a big step towards China's semiconductor biz standing on its own two feet. It takes a complicated lithographic machine to produce a modern chip, and there are two main types: EUV (Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography) and DUV (Deep Ultraviolet Lithography). It's the older of the two, DUV, that a Chinese company is said to have figured out. These sorts of immersion machines are still used for modern computer chips, and today most are made by Dutch company ASML, which took over from the Japanese companies that dominated prior. Citing people familiar with the matter, The Information says the Chinese DUV machines are set to be delivered to customers this year . Customers including, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp., Hua Hong Semiconductor, and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). Yeah, that same CXMT everyone is talking about due to surging memory costs. While this does challenge ASML for the sale of DUV machines in China, the machines are said to be lagging behind in performance and reliability. This news comes at a time when a plan to restrict sale…

body: Jay and Silent Bob first appeared in the 1994 grunge film Clerks as eccentric weed dealers. Jay was the sweary, loquacious, long haired slacker, and Silent Bob was the silent, ruminative long haired slacker. They were cult figures in the '90s. Most of my teenage friends thought they were very funny, and Clerks is still a fun time capsule of the early '90s. But like a lot of '90s phenomena, Jay and Silent Bob quickly contorted into parody. They've spawned at least three standalone films, each more silly than the last. They also reliably feature in every one of Kevin Smith's View Asknewiverse films, from Clerks all the way through to Clerks 3, but also taking in Mallrats, Chasing Amy and Dogma, just to name a handful. More recently they've started getting their own videogames: Jay and Silent Bob Mall Brawl is a 2020 sidescrolling beat 'em up developed for NES but also ported to PC and consoles. In April, Atari published Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch , which is also a sidescrolling beat 'em up but with a modern comic book presentation. body: In June, Sjoerd De Jong—an Unreal Engine modder and map creator turned full-time specialist at Epic Games— announced that he was leaving the company after 12 years as a senior director and Unreal Engine "lead evangelist." In a cryptic departure message, he said the games industry was at a "pivotal point," and he's aiming to "work out how to adapt and excel" at addressing the changing needs of videogame development. We now have a clearer idea of De Jong's plans for navigating the games industry's future. In an interview with This Week in Videogames , De Jong revealed what he's tackling next: He's building a game engine of his own. De Jong's nascent game engine competitor is called the Immens Engine, and he's building it alongside a small team of co-founders that includes former Epic technical director Arjan Brussee. De Jong intends for Immens to serve as an alternative to the dominance of Unreal and Unity, whose market influence he said has led to a "stagnation" in game development for which challengers like Godot have only just recently started to emerge. title: Vatican scrambles to patch 'phishing goldmine' app promoted by the Pope: 'Prayer infrastructure on the framework you learn in week 2 of a Node.js bootcamp'
summary: Jesus Christ.
body: On January 20, 2019, Pope Francis delivered his weekly Angelus to St Peter's Square from a window in the Vatican's Apostolic Palace. In it, he enjoined the faithful to join him on the Church's then-new Click To Pray app—helpfully modelled by a nearby priest, wielding a tablet. Hundreds of thousands of people signed up in the years that followed. But maybe they shouldn't have, because it turns out the Click To Pray app was, until very recently, absolutely rife with info-leaking security holes. White-hat hacker BobDaHacker revealed in a July 24 blog post (via The Register ) that "The Pope's official app exposes 700,000+ user emails." The vulnerability has since been fixed, but it seems only after BobDaHacker went public with their investigation—inquiries made by the hacker and by journalists stretching back to January this year went unanswered. The vulnerability itself was pretty simple. When you sign up for Click To Pray, the site hands your user account an ID number. The first guy to sign up was one, the next was two, and so on, all the way into the hundreds of thousands. Problem is, by visiting https://api.clicktopray.org/user/users/[ID number goes here] , you could retrieve the …

title: Micron's low power DRAM 'consumes approximately one-third the power of DDR5' in AI data center workloads, but I'm not sure that's good news
summary: Micron finds LPDDR5X can account for less than 7% of total system power.
body: AI's hunger for both power and memory, plus the resulting supply crisis of the latter, has led to many industry players engaging in a spot of creative problem solving. Case in point, Micron and Meta have collaborated on an experimental data centre roll out of low power DRAM. Micron has developed SOCAMM2 , a fresh form factor for LPDDR5X that is a "modular, serviceable module designed for servers." Testing used "Meta’s open-source DCPerf benchmark suite, which reflects production environments across a hyperscale fleet," and found that this low-power DRAM module "consumes approximately one-third the power of DDR5." According to Micron's white paper report , that accounts for under 7% of total system power. The white paper goes on to elaborate that LPDDR5X's "reduced operating voltage and advanced signalling allows bandwidth to scale without a corresponding rise in power consumption, resulting in better bandwidth-per-watt performance than conventional server memory." Basically, data centres can install more low power DRAM without also hiking up power-related operating costs. The AI industry potentially switching away from DDR5 may sound like good news in the short term for memory-sta…

Despite it all, I loved it. Stalker 2 had the bones of something beautiful, just as soon as GSC could get around to, you know, finishing making it. If that time hasn't arrived, I think it's fast-approaching. On August 20, almost two years after the base game's release, Stalker 2 will get its first expansion, Cost of Hope . This is the first of two planned story DLCs for the game, this one focusing on the Zone's Duty (who think the Zone is scary and we should shoot it), and Freedom (who think the Zone is wondrous and we should share it) factions. title: Jensen Huang's first-ever post on X is in defense of open access to AI models, alongside Google, OpenAI, and Meta
summary: Many companies argue a bad guy with an open AI is best fought by a good guy with an open AI.
body: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang joined X last month, and recently made his first-ever post . As you could probably guess, it's about AI. He argues, alongside companies like Google, OpenAI, and Meta, that the US should not aim to restrict open models 'prematurely', as they're important for the growth of AI (among other things). Taking a quick step back, Open models are ones that give access to weights or even code to see how it runs and to allow users to modify them. These can be run locally and are customisable. Closed models are those that tend to be run by specific companies, accessed via the cloud and APIs, and keep all their weights hidden. Open models out of China, like DeepSeek, became a problem for American AI firms at the start of last year. They exploded onto the scene, offering similar services to the likes of OpenAI, but totally free and available locally. Just last week, the Trump administration was reportedly looking to ban Chinese AI models due to cybersecurity concerns. The battle between closed and open models is also partially a digital proxy war between American and non-American AI. Open models give access to anyone, and the US is hoping for AI dominance. Sharing how i…

body: On Monday, Chinese memory manufacturer CXMT made its initial public offering on Shanghai's STAR stock market. This debut was the biggest in Asia this year, raising $8.6 billion and seeing shares in the company surge by 466%. In terms of valuation, that places CXMT right at the top of China's stock market. CXMT's market capitalisation is now about $487.73 billion. Major player Tencent still outpaces it at a little over $500 billion, but that makes CXMT's stock market debut no less show-stealing. In fact, according to Reuters , the memory manufacturer is now a more valuable listed company than even the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. Even before this news, CXMT was already one to watch; the company's plans to massively ramp up DRAM manufacturing capacity in the midst of the RAMpocalypse has made its products an appealing option for a number of PC component makers . Furthermore, recent reports suggest that CXMT is planning to expand overseas into the US market at some point in the future. CXMT's rise may be far from unstoppable, though. body: Qualcomm, the company behind the Snapdragon chips you will find in many phones, Windows on Arm laptops, and VR headsets, is reportedly raising its prices starting September 1. Unfortunately, that could mean bad news for both WoA and future VR headsets. This is according to a letter sent to customers on Friday, which was seen by Bloomberg . According to that document, the price increase will be a percentage in the double digits, and presumably, that rise will only worsen the price of the devices that use the company's chips. One such device is Valve's Steam Frame , which rocks a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and is said to be launching soon. The Steam Frame is its new wireless VR headset, and one designed for game streaming. It uses a special dongle for foveated streaming, which delivers the parts you are looking at in higher quality, saving on bandwidth. Steam has said all three pieces of its hardware triumvirate (Steam Controller, Steam Machine, and Steam Frame) would launch by the end of Summer, which means we have around a month left before that self-imposed deadline. summary: In fairness, I have a lot of unfinished things marked JOSH TO-DO going back to 2011 as well.
body: I've said it before and, in all likelihood, will say it again several more times: one of the best things about PC gaming is that modders can come in long after a game has been set aside by its developers, and proceed to clean up all the nagging bugs and imperfections that continue to linger. Take, for example, MGSHDFix , which sprang into existence not longer after the initial launch of the Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol 1 to spruce up MGS2 and 3 (plus MG1 and 2) ports that were, at the time, lackluster. Konami's done a lot of work on the games since then, and they're in a good state, but there's always work to be done. That's why MGSHDFix 4.0.0 released over the weekend. It's a doozy. "With MGSHDFix 4.0.0, MGS2 is effectively restored back to its original pre-HD Collection state," writes author Afevis. "All of MGS2's graphical effects that Bluepoint left unimplemented (there was a ton of things that were literally left marked as 'BLUEPOINT TO-DO' still in the source code that are still untouched to today), have been fully restored (either through the game's own rendering system, or in some cases, through modern custom D3D11 recreations.)" body: The flood of retail simulators on Steam is nothing new: the trend seemed to land with torrential force in late 2024. But it's fascinating, to me at least, how many of these things are still being released every week, and how many of them seem to actually reach an audience despite their rudimentary appearance. Last week, 14 retail sims were released on Steam. I'm being pretty picky with what I class a "retail sim" too. If it's an idle game with a retail or service industry theme, it's not included. If it's a horror game with a retail setting—and there are tons of these, including this week's Shift at Midnight—they're not included either. If it's a puzzle game with retail or service industry themes, like Nothing To Declare , I'm not including it. No, I'm talking about those unfailingly first-person retail sims that extremely prolific Polish publisher PlayWay seemed to spawn into existence, and which have been copied relentlessly since (including by PlayWay itself). title: If you miss the straightforward action RPGs of the past, try the generous demo for Darkstone Restoration
summary: Open a portal, we're going back.
body: Before action RPGs relied on seasonal ladders and DLC treadmills there was Darkstone, a 1999 hack and slash where you clicked on things until they died and liked it. It had some interesting ideas, like the companion mode that lets you switch between two player-characters, the other controlled by the CPU while you took the lead, but it remained true to the basics of a genre I got into precisely because it was basic. Now it's back, with a remaster in early access that improves the UI and controls (you can move characters with WASD now, or play with a controller), and the graphics (though I had to turn off volumetric fog and procedural grass for the sake of my poor framerate). It's got a demo too, which lets you make characters from any of its eight classes and explore the early-game dungeons, letting you play three of its quests, which are selected at random each time you start a new game. It's just nice to start up an action RPG without having to worry about which build I'm going to pursue, or look at a massive node full of future skill unlocks, or wonder if I should start a seasonal character or whether I'm missing out by not buying the latest DLC. Darkstone is just Darkstone, a g…

title: J.K. Simmons hasn't played Baldur's Gate 3 or any of his games, but he loves Portal 2: 'I could have done the feature film, or the play, or whatever'

body: In a recent appearance on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , prolific actor J.K. Simmons dove into his relationship with the games he's acted in. "He said, 'I'm about to kill you.' Okay, well, good luck with that." Host Josh Horowitz followed up by asking if Simmons enjoys playing games at all, and the answer was a firm no. "My hands don't work on those controllers," said Simmons. "I've tried⁠—my kids, of course, my twentysomething kids play them a lot. But even if he doesn't play, Simmons does have a firm favorite among all the games he's acted in. "It was Portal 2, for me," he said. "Just because it was such a hilarious script. title: How do you feel about AI videogame music?
summary: Does your music require the human touch?
body: Like it or loathe it—and for the record, I am firmly in the latter camp–generative AI has continued to seep into every aspect of game development. What felt like the odd shovelware AI thumbnail here or generated texture there has transformed into "developers" parading around entirely vibe-coded videogames as if it's something to be celebrated, rather than looked upon with sheer horror at the willing dismantling of human creativity and spirit. Critical Hit (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Critical Hit , where I (or someone else on the PC Gamer team) celebrate and lament all things videogame music, audio design, and the ways our favourite games make our ears tingle. While videogame music has still largely held off from falling to generative AI, that doesn't mean it's not happening. YouTube has already become plagued with so-called "rearrangements" of beloved videogame scores that are, unsurprisingly, concocted entirely by a LLM. Spotify has been under intense scrutiny for the immense flooding of AI music across the platform—as well as fielding accusations that it's been planting AI-generated music it owns in its official playlists as a way to pay real artists less money. summary: "The grey, misty gloom streaking past me is authentically British."
body: (Image credit: Dovetail Games) I've taken the train from Bath to London hundreds of times in my life, usually to visit game developers in the capital. And while I enjoy that part of the job, the journey itself is a dispiriting chore. Rail travel in the United Kingdom is a chaos of delays, overcrowding and overpriced sandwiches. Yet when I saw Great Western Express on Steam—an expansion for Train Sim World that recreates part of that route—I felt compelled to play it. Videogames are a powerful form of escapism for me, but what if I played one to achieve the complete opposite of that? Train Sim World is primarily a game about driving trains, but it's unique in that it also lets you be a passenger. Bath isn't in the game yet, so I start my journey at Reading, and I'm immediately struck by how well they've recreated the station. I've spent many hours here over the years waiting for delayed connections, and the layout is perfect—although the lack of a pasty shop is jarring. The pasty is a station staple, and I will forever associate the smell of hot pastry with waiting for trains. On Rails I get on the train and it's a strange experience seeing something so mundane, so tediously everyd…

title: Larian once again reminds us it's 'not involved in any BG3-related projects' in response to Karlach comic reveal
summary: Dispelling any doubt on the matter.
body: Larian Studios has reiterated that it is fully, 100%, without a doubt, donezo in the bunzo when it comes to new Baldur's Gate-related projects. It's latest statement was in response to a Dark Horse comics announcement that could have been interpreted as implying the studio's involvement. Maximum hijinks are happening right now, but we’re not involved in any BG3 related projects.As soon as we bust outta here, we'll share more about @divinity https://t.co/SANGQ82QZ8 pic.twitter.com/v75lPYljU8 July 25, 2026 On X, "The Everything App," Dark Horse announced that a yet-untitled comic series starring Karlach , our favorite BG3 companion, is coming down the pike. The issue: Dark Horse signed off its post by saying the project was "With [Larian] and [Wizards of the Coast]," tagging both companies. Makes sense. I mean, Larian famously did make Baldur's Gate 3 and the character of Karlach in the first place. But the studio seems keen to head off any suggestion that it is involved in Wizards of the Coast's post-BG3 spinoff projects. title: Videogame villains who sing at you are the best
summary: The Devil has all the best tunes. But GLaDOS has some good ones too.
body: Villains monologue at us so much in videogames it's become passe. Oh, you're so evil you took over the radio station and replaced the friendly voice that's been guiding me since the tutorial just so you can tell me about your evil plan? Yawn. Use that radio to sing a song at me, maybe then I'll pay attention. Sing during a boss fight and I'll pay even more attention. I'm not sure where this trend started, but the videogame boss who is so extra they can't help but perform an entire song-and-dance routine while kicking your ass has become a delightful trend—though not all the entries on this list are boss-fight songs. If it happened too often it would stop being surprising and lose all its power. Which is also why games that are entirely musical don't count for the purpose of this list. You won't find Stray Gods, Billie Bust Up, Rhapsody: A Musical Adventure, No Straight Roads, People of Note, or Mortimer and the Riddles of the Medallion here. Only unexpected songs count, which is why you shouldn't read this list if you don't want their existence spoiled for you.
